sec.title: Background
sec.p: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a common neurocognitive complication following surgery, particularly in older adults. Esketamine has been investigated for potential neuroprotective effects in the perioperative setting. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effect of perioperative esketamine on the incidence of POD.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A comprehensive literature search was conducted across multiple electronic databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, and Google Scholar) to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the association between perioperative esketamine administration and POD. The primary outcome was the incidence of POD. Secondary outcomes included postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD), delayed neurocognitive recovery (dNCR), postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), length of hospital stay, length of post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) stay, and postoperative pain in the first 24 h after surgery. PROSPERO registration: CRD42024587392.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: 25 RCTs involving 3,669 participants were included (esketamine: 17 trials; ketamine: 8 trials). Esketamine was associated with a lower incidence of POD (risk ratio [RR]: 0.55, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.46–0.67, P < 0.00001), whereas ketamine showed no significant effect (RR: 0.64, 95% CI: 0.32–1.29, P = 0.21). Results were consistent in studies enrolling elderly patients (≥ 65 years) (RR: 0.57, 95% CI: 0.41–0.80, P = 0.001). Esketamine was also associated with a lower risk of PONV and reduced pain within 24 h after surgery. No significant differences were observed in hospital or PACU length of stay.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Perioperative administration of esketamine was associated with significantly lower incidence of POD, without concomitant increases in length of hospital or PACU stay.

abstract.title: Highlights
abstract.p: 1. Perioperative administration of esketamine was associated with significantly reduced incidence of postoperative delirium.
2. Secondary analysis demonstrated that ketamine administration was not associated with a significant reduction in the incidence of postoperative delirium.
3. Our study revealed no significant increase in hospital or post-anesthesia care unit stay associated with esketamine use.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Postoperative delirium (POD) represents a significant complication affecting patients across various surgical procedures, with reported incidence rates ranging from 15 to 80% depending on the patient population, surgical type, and diagnostic criteria employed [1, 2]. This acute neuropsychiatric disorder manifests as fluctuating disturbances in attention, awareness, and cognition, typically developing within the first seven postoperative days [3]. POD is associated with prolonged hospital stays, increased healthcare costs, higher mortality rates, and long-term cognitive decline [4, 5]. The pathophysiology of POD remains incompletely understood but involves multiple mechanisms including neuroinflammation, neurotransmitter imbalances, oxidative stress, and disruption of cerebral metabolism [6].

Given the substantial burden of POD on healthcare systems and patient outcomes, identification of effective preventive strategies has emerged as a clinical research priority. Current preventive approaches for POD emphasize multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions as first-line measures, although their implementation can be resource-intensive and their efficacy uncertain [7]. Pharmacological prophylaxis remains controversial, with numerous agents investigated yielding inconsistent results [8, 9]. In this context, the search for effective pharmacological agents with favorable risk–benefit profiles continues to be an active area of investigation.

Ketamine, an non-competitive N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist with unique pharmacodynamic properties, has garnered increasing attention as a potential agent for POD prevention [10]. Traditionally utilized as an anesthetic and analgesic, ketamine has shown neuroprotective effects through multiple mechanisms including anti-inflammatory properties, reduction of excitotoxicity, and preservation of cerebral blood flow [11–13]. Its S-enantiomer, esketamine, possesses similar mechanisms of action with potentially enhanced potency and fewer adverse effects [14, 15]. The theoretical framework supporting the potential role of ketamine or esketamine in POD prevention is compelling. However, clinical evidence remains fragmented and contradictory [16, 17].

Several studies have suggested that sub-anesthetic doses of ketamine (0.15–0.5 mg/kg) may reduce perioperative cognitive dysfunction [18], while others have found no significant benefit or even potential harm [19]. The 2018 American Society for Enhanced Recovery and Perioperative Quality Initiative Joint Consensus Statement on Postoperative Delirium Prevention guidelines neither specifically recommend nor contraindicate the use of ketamine for POD prophylaxis, largely due to limited and heterogenous evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) [20]. Since then, additional RCTs have been published, warranting a comprehensive reassessment of the available evidence. The clinical heterogeneity in existing studies regarding ketamine dosing regimens, timing of administration, patient populations, and tools of POD assessment has complicated interpretation of the current literature and hindered development of evidence-based recommendations. Moreover, the emergence of esketamine as a potential alternative to ketamine necessitates evaluation of its efficacy in POD prevention [21, 22].

Given the high prevalence and detrimental consequences of POD, along with the increasing use of ketamine or esketamine in multimodal analgesic strategies, there is a critical need to clarify the relationship between perioperative ketamine or esketamine administration and POD. Therefore, we conducted this systematic review and meta-analysis to comprehensively evaluate whether perioperative administration of ketamine or esketamine reduces the incidence of POD compared to controls. Secondary objectives included assessment of the effect of esketamine on postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD), delayed neurocognitive recovery (dNCR), postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), length of hospital stay, length of post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) stay and postoperative pain in the first 24 h after surgery.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024587392). We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement for reporting the results and the Assessment of Multiple Systematic Reviews (AMSTAR) guidelines for methodological quality evaluation [23, 24].

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: Utilizing the Population/Intervention/Comparator/Outcome (PICO) framework, studies were selected based on the following criteria: Population comprised adult patients (≥ 18 years) undergoing general anesthesia; Intervention involved intravenous administration of ketamine or esketamine without restrictions regarding dosage or delivery protocol; Comparator consisted of placebo, non-intervention, or alternative pharmacological agents; and Outcome measured was POD. Only peer-reviewed RCTs were considered eligible regardless of publication language.

Exclusion criteria encompassed: (1) non-randomized designs including observational studies, animal studies, case reports, conference abstracts, editorials and reviews; (2) protocols with inadequate description about ketamine or esketamine regimens; (3) investigations that failed to report POD incidence; and (4) studies including patients undergoing procedural sedation rather than general anesthesia.

sec.title: Outcome measures
sec.p: The primary outcome was the incidence of POD. Secondary outcomes comprised POCD, dNCR, PONV, length of hospital stay, length of PACU stay, and postoperative pain in the first 24 h after surgery as quantified via patient-reported instruments including the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) or Numerical Rating Scale (NRS).

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: To ensure a comprehensive identification of relevant studies examining the effect of intravenous ketamine or esketamine on POD, a systematic search was conducted across multiple electronic databases with no language restriction, including PubMed, the Cochrane Library, EMBASE, and Google Scholar. The search strategy incorporated a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text terms related to “ketamine”, “esketamine”, “surgery”, “anaesthesia”, and “RCT”. To minimize the risk of missing pertinent studies, the reference lists of eligible articles and relevant systematic reviews were manually screened. The literature search was conducted from database inception to January 20, 2026, to ensure inclusion of the most recent evidence. A detailed summary of the search terms is provided in Supplementary Table S1. Our search was last updated in January 2026, and therefore, the most recent studies published afterward may not have been included.

sec.title: Study selection process
sec.p: Two investigators independently conducted a preliminary screening of titles and abstracts from all retrieved citations. Articles meeting predetermined eligibility criteria or demonstrating insufficient information for definitive exclusion underwent subsequent full-text evaluation. Discordant assessments between reviewers were reconciled through consensus discussion or, when necessary, adjudication by a third senior investigator.

sec.title: Data extraction and quality assessment
sec.p: A standardized data extraction form was developed to ensure uniformity in data collection across all included studies. Extracted variables included first and corresponding authors, publication year, journal, country, study period, population characteristics, baseline demographics (age, sex), sample size, surgical type, ketamine or esketamine administration modalities, timing and method of POD assessment, and follow-up duration. When necessary data were unavailable, corresponding authors were contacted to obtain additional information. The methodological quality and potential biases of the included RCTs were systematically assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool [25]. Two investigators independently evaluated each study across seven domains: (1) random sequence generation (selection bias), (2) allocation concealment (selection bias), (3) blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias), (4) blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias), (5) incomplete outcome data (attrition bias), (6) selective reporting (reporting bias), and (7) other potential sources of biases. Following the prescribed standards, each domain was classified as having “low risk”, “unclear risk”, or “high risk” of bias. Overall risk-of-bias judgments were assigned as follows: studies with low risk ratings across all domains received an overall “low risk” designation; studies with one or more domains rated as “unclear risk” but no “high risk” domains received an overall classification of “unclear risk”; and any study with at least one domain assessed as “high risk” was assigned an overall “high risk” of bias designation [25]. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) method was utilized to assess the certainty of evidence for primary and secondary outcomes [26]. Five domains were evaluated: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Evidence quality assessment was performed using GRADEpro version 3.6 software (McMaster University, 2014).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using Review Manager software (RevMan, version 5.3; The Cochrane Collaboration, Copenhagen, Denmark) and R software (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). All extracted data were visualized through forest plots.

For dichotomous outcomes, effect estimates were expressed as pooled risk ratios (RRs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Continuous variables were analyzed using either mean differences (MDs) when outcomes were measured on the same scale or standardized mean differences (SMDs) when different measurement scales were employed across studies, both presented with their respective 95% CIs. The included studies employed two different pain assessment instruments to evaluate pain intensity within the initial 24-h after surgery: VAS and NRS. To facilitate quantitative synthesis of these heterogeneous measurement tools, we standardized the reported outcomes by calculating SMDs. Additionally, a cumulative meta-analysis was conducted, sequentially incorporating studies according to their chronological publication order to evaluate the evolution of evidence over time.

Between-study heterogeneity was quantitatively assessed using the I2 statistic. In accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, heterogeneity was classified as follows: I2 values < 25% indicated minimal heterogeneity; values between 25 and 50% represented moderate heterogeneity; values between 50 and 75% denoted substantial heterogeneity; and values > 75% signified considerable heterogeneity. When significant heterogeneity was detected (I2 > 50%), a random-effects model (DerSimonian and Laird method) was applied; otherwise, a fixed-effects model (Mantel–Haenszel method) was employed for data synthesis.

The primary objective of this meta-analysis was to evaluate the effect of esketamine administration on the incidence of POD. The secondary objective was to assess the effects of ketamine on POD and of esketamine on POCD, dNCR, PONV, hospital length of stay, PACU stay, and postoperative pain within 24 h after surgery.

Sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate the stability of pooled estimates by sequentially omitting individual studies and recalculating the summary effect estimate. This approach allowed assessment of whether any single study exerted disproportionate influence on the overall results of meta-analysis. Pre-specified sensitivity analyses were performed by restricting the pooled analysis to studies enrolling elderly patients (≥ 65 years) and studies with POD follow-up of ≥ 3 days. For outcomes with contributions from more than ten studies, potential publication bias and small-study effects were formally evaluated through visual inspection of funnel plot asymmetry and quantified using Egger’s regression test. Additionally, the trim-and-fill method was applied to adjust for potential publication bias when detected.

There was substantial variability in esketamine dosing across the included studies. Accordingly, we investigated the association between esketamine dosage and treatment effect using meta-regression analysis. For these analyses, bolus and infusion doses were combined to estimate total dosage. When both were administered, total dosage was calculated by summing the bolus dose and the infusion dose assuming a minimum surgical duration of 1 h (e.g., a bolus of 0.5 mg/kg plus an infusion of 0.5 mg/kg/h was considered a total dose of 1.0 mg/kg).
Throughout all statistical analyses, a two-sided alpha level of 0.05 was established as the threshold for statistical significance.

sec.title: Selection process
sec.p: The selection process is illustrated in Fig. 1. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across PubMed, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, Google Scholar and web pages, yielding 3,381 records. Following removal of 618 duplicates, 2,758 articles remained for initial screening. After reviewing titles and abstracts, 2,689 records were excluded. The full texts of the remaining 69 articles were thoroughly evaluated for eligibility, resulting in the exclusion of 44 studies due to: non-RCT design (n = 6), sedation rather than general anesthesia (n = 12), absence of POD incidence data (n = 2), incorrect outcome (n = 23), and inaccessible full text (n = 1). The final analysis included 25 eligible RCTs comprising 3,669 patients; 17 studies evaluated esketamine and 8 evaluated ketamine.

sec.title: Study characteristics
sec.p: The characteristics of the 17 included studies are summarized in Table 1. All studies were published between 2022 and 2025 and included a total of 2,291 patients, with individual sample sizes ranging from 60 to 372 participants. Average age of participants across studies ranged from 51 to 80 years. Sex distribution varied substantially, with the proportion of male participants ranging from 0% in studies enrolling only females undergoing breast surgery to 77.4% in mixed-sex cohorts. Surgical procedures including gastrointestinal (29.4%, 5/17) [27–30], thoracic (23.5%, 4/17) [31–34], orthopedic (11.8%, 2/17) [35, 36], cardiac (11.8%, 2/17) [37, 38], and mastectomy (11.8%, 2/17) [39, 40] surgeries, while two studies (11.8%, 2/17) [41, 42] included multiple surgical types. Esketamine was administered intraoperatively in most studies (64.7%, 11/17), one study (5.9%) used esketamine exclusively for postoperative analgesia, and five studies (29.4%) administered esketamine both intraoperatively and postoperatively. Dosing regimens varied, with loading doses ranging from 0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg and continuous infusion rates from 0.1 to 0.25 mg/kg/h. POD was assessed using validated instruments, including the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM), CAM for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU), Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). Follow-up durations ranged from 1 to 7 days postoperatively.

sec.title: Quality assessment of included studies
sec.p: Risk of bias assessment for individual studies was illustrated in Fig. 2. Eleven investigations (64.7%) demonstrated low overall risk of bias, indicating methodological rigor and enhanced reliability of reported outcomes. Three studies (17.6%) had unclear risk of bias, suggesting insufficient information for comprehensive bias assessment in one or more domains. Three studies (17.6%) exhibited high overall risk of bias, potentially compromising the validity of our findings. Among the domains assessed, allocation concealment was the most common source of high risk of bias (n = 3 studies). The three studies with unclear risk typically had insufficient details reported regarding blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias) or blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias), precluding definitive judgment.

sec.title: Incidence of POD
sec.p: Meta-analysis demonstrated a significantly reduced incidence of POD in the intervention group compared with controls (RR: 0.55, 95% CI: 0.46–0.67, P < 0.00001), with no observed heterogeneity (I2 = 0%) (Fig. 3). Cumulative meta-analysis using a fixed-effects model illustrated the temporal evolution of effect estimates as sequential studies were incorporated (Supplementary Fig. 1). Effect size estimates exhibited progressive stabilization with study accumulation, while concurrent narrowing of CIs reflected enhanced precision of the pooled estimate. The cumulative meta-analysis further delineated the chronological point at which statistical significance was initially achieved and subsequently maintained. Secondary analysis showed that ketamine administration was not associated with a statistically significant reduction in POD incidence (RR: 0.64, 95% CI: 0.32–1.29, P = 0.21), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 60%) (Fig. 4).

sec.title: Incidence of POCD and dNCR
sec.p: Data on POCD incidence were available from only three studies (17.6% of included trials), comprising 402 patients. Meta-analysis revealed a statistical reduction in POCD incidence in the intervention group (RR: 0.62, 95% CI: 0.45–0.86, P = 0.004), with moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 49%) (Supplementary Fig. 2). Data on dNCR were reported in only two studies (11.8%) including 157 patients. Meta-analysis also indicated a lower incidence of dNCR in the intervention group (RR: 0.28, 95% CI: 0.13–0.60, P = 0.001), with moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 31%) (Supplementary Fig. 3). However, given the limited number of small studies, the current evidence remains insufficient to support definitive clinical conclusions regarding POCD or dNCR.

sec.title: Incidence of PONV
sec.p: PONV were reported in ten studies (58.8%). Meta-analysis showed that esketamine administration was associated with a significantly lower risk of PONV compared with control interventions (RR: 0.78, 95% CI: 0.63–0.96, P = 0.02), with no observed heterogeneity (I2 = 0%) (Supplementary Fig. 4).

sec.title: Length of hospital stay and PACU stay
sec.p: Length of hospital stay was reported in four studies (23.5%), including 746 patients. Perioperative esketamine administration was not associated with a significant difference in hospital length of stay compared with controls (MD: -0.87 days, 95% CI: -1.95 to 0.20 days, P = 0.11), with considerable heterogeneity observed (I2 = 90%) (Supplementary Fig. 5). Similarly, length of PACU stay, reported in five studies (n = 736), showed no significant between-group difference (MD: -3.61 min, 95% CI: -7.85 to 0.62 min, P = 0.09, I2 = 93%) (Supplementary Fig. 6).

sec.title: Pain scores at 24 h after surgery
sec.p: Postoperative pain within the first 24 h after surgery was reported in nine studies (52.9%). Pain intensity was assessed using validated instruments, including VAS (55.6%, 5/9) and NRS (44.4%, 4/9). Meta-analysis demonstrated significantly lower pain scores at 24 h postoperatively in the esketamine group compared with controls (SMD: -0.61, 95% CI: -0.88 to -0.33, P < 0.0001), with considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 77%) (Supplementary Fig. 7). The observed SMD of -0.61 corresponds to a moderate effect size according to Cohen’s criteria (where SMD of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 represent small, moderate, and large effects, respectively).

sec.title: Sensitivity analysis and publication bias
sec.p: Sensitivity analyses employing a leave-one-out method demonstrated robustness of the primary findings (Supplementary Fig. 8). Analysis restricted to studies enrolling elderly patients (≥ 65 years) and studies with extended POD follow-up (≥ 3 days) yielded results that were generally consistent with the main analysis (RR: 0.57, 95% CI: 0.41–0.80, P = 0.001; RR: 0.55, 95% CI: 0.45–0.67, P < 0.00001) (Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 9). Moreover, post hoc sensitivity analyses excluding studies rated as high risk of bias were performed, which yield results consistent with the primary analysis (RR: 0.57, 95% CI: 0.47–0.70, P < 0.00001), suggesting that these high-risk studies did not disproportionately influence the overall findings (Supplementary Fig. 10). Supplementary Fig. 11 presented the funnel plot assessment of publication bias, revealing symmetrical distribution suggestive of minimal publication bias. Egger’s regression analysis further supported the absence of publication bias for the POD outcome (P = 0.9413).

caption.p: Forest plot showing the impact of esketamine on POD in elderly patients (≥ 65 years). CI, confidence interval; df, degrees of freedom

sec.title: Meta-regression
sec.p: Meta-regression analysis was performed to assess the association between esketamine dosage and effect size, thereby exploring potential dose–response relationships. Across the included studies, total esketamine dose ranged from 0.25 to 0.55 mg/kg in most trials, with one study administering 1.0 mg/kg and another 1.5 mg/kg. The meta-regression analysis did not identify a statistically significant association between esketamine dose and effect size (coefficient = 0.53, P = 0.347; Supplementary Fig. 12), suggesting a comparable protective effect against POD across the examined dose range.

sec.title: Grading the quality of evidence
sec.p: According to the GRADE framework, the certainty of evidence for the effects of esketamine on POD and PONV was rated as moderate. In contrast, the evidence for POCD, dNCR, hospital length of stay, PACU stay, and 24-h postoperative pain was rated as low. sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated 25 RCTs involving 3,669 patients, examining the effect of esketamine and ketamine on POD. We provided a moderate-level certainty that administration of esketamine significantly reduced POD incidence. Additionally, esketamine administration was associated with decreased risk of POCD, dNCR, PONV, and attenuated pain scores at 24 h postoperatively. No significant differences were detected between the esketamine and control groups in length of hospital stay or PACU stay. Secondary analyses also indicated that ketamine administration was not associated with reduced incidence of POD.

Our meta-analysis demonstrated that esketamine administration significantly reduced POD incidence, a clinically meaningful finding given limited prophylactic interventions available for this neurocognitive complication. Multiple mechanisms account for the observed beneficial effect. First, esketamine function as NMDA receptor antagonists that inhibit the toll-like receptor 4/nuclear factor kappa B (TLR4/NF-ĸB) signaling pathway in microglial cells [43], resulting in decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine production, attenuated neuroinflammatory cascade activation, and subsequent improvement of postoperative cognitive function. Second, postoperative pain and opioid consumption are well-established risk factors for POD development in the surgical population [44]. Esketamine demonstrated significant analgesic efficacy, as evidenced by reduced postoperative pain intensity scores and decreased cumulative opioid requirements [45–47]. This opioid-sparing effect potentially mitigates opioid-induced neurotoxicity, which may contribute to the observed reduction in POD incidence. Third, esketamine exhibits antidepressant properties mediated through glutamatergic modulation and downstream effects on brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression [48–51]. These neurochemical alterations may attenuate perioperative psychological distress and affective dysregulation, potentially contributing to POD prophylaxis. The multifaceted pharmacodynamic profile of esketamine encompassing anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and neuromodulatory mechanisms appears to confer neuroprotective benefits that may help prevent perioperative cognitive dysfunction [52].

Current perioperative guidelines emphasize multimodal strategies for POD prevention, particularly within Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathways. One key component of these protocols is the avoidance or minimization of benzodiazepines, which have been consistently associated with increased delirium risk, especially in older surgical patients. Consequently, many ERAS recommendations advocate alternative sedative and analgesic approaches to reduce exposure to benzodiazepines in the perioperative period. Among pharmacologic strategies, dexmedetomidine has demonstrated relatively consistent evidence for delirium prevention. Meta-analyses of RCTs suggest that dexmedetomidine may reduce the risk of POD with a pooled RR of approximately 0.67, particularly in critically ill or high-risk surgical populations [53]. Compared with this evidence base, the findings for esketamine remain less consistent. Therefore, esketamine should be considered within the broader context of established delirium prevention strategies, including benzodiazepine avoidance, optimized analgesia, sleep promotion, and early mobilization, while further research is needed to clarify the role of NMDA receptor antagonists in this setting.

Several recent meta-analyses have investigated the efficacy of ketamine or esketamine in relation to perioperative neurocognitive outcomes. Notably, Santos Neto et al. [54] examined the preventative effects of ketamine or esketamine on POD in surgical populations, while Su et al. [55] and Xu et al. [56] focused predominantly on esketamine and its association with broader perioperative neurocognitive outcomes such as POCD or dNCR. Our study differs from these analyses in several important ways. First, we evaluated both esketamine and ketamine, allowing direct comparison between the two agents. Second, our analysis specifically focused on POD as the primary outcome, which remains one of the most clinically significant neurocognitive complications after surgery. Third, meta-regression analyses were performed to assess the impact of varying dosages of esketamine on the observed effect size. Finally, our updated search included recently published RCTs that were not incorporated in earlier reviews. Despite these differences, our findings are broadly consistent with prior evidence suggesting a potential benefit of esketamine for POD prevention, while evidence supporting ketamine remains limited.

While the statistical heterogeneity observed in the pooled analysis was minimal ((I2 = 0%), considerable clinical heterogeneity existed among the included studies. The trials varied in several aspects, including types of surgical procedures, esketamine dosing regimens, timing of drug administration, and patient populations. These variations may influence the observed treatment effects and limit the comparability across studies. Consequently, although the pooled results suggest a potential benefit of esketamine in reducing POD, the substantial clinical heterogeneity limits the ability to make specific dosing or administration recommendations for routine clinical practice.

According to the updated nomenclature recommendations [3], POCD refers to cognitive decline diagnosed up to 12 months following surgery, whereas dNCR is defined as cognitive decline identified within 30 days postoperatively. In the present analysis, a statistically significant reduction was observed for both POD and dNCR. However, given the small number of studies, heterogeneous neuropsychological assessments and low-certainty evidence, definitive recommendations regarding long-term neurocognitive protection cannot be made at this time. Future large-scale prospective RCTs incorporating standardized neuropsychological testing batteries and extended follow-up protocols are needed to better define the long-term cognitive effects of esketamine.

In present study, administration of esketamine was associated with a significant reduction in postoperative pain scores, aligned with recent systematic reviews demonstrating NMDA receptor antagonists could attenuate acute postoperative pain intensity [45, 47]. The analgesic properties of esketamine are primarily attributed to NMDA receptor antagonism, effectively preventing the development of central sensitization and mitigating opioid-induced hyperalgesia [57, 58]. The observed standardized effect size (SMD = -0.61) represents a moderate effect according to conventional benchmarks. However, given the considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 77%) and variation in pain assessment tools, this conclusion should be interpreted with caution. With respect to potential adverse effects associated with esketamine administration, our analysis demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in PONV incidence among patients receiving esketamine. This unexpected finding may be attributed to the opioid-sparing properties of esketamine, which reduce perioperative opioid requirements. The observed reduction in PONV suggested potential benefits of esketamine for postoperative recovery. In addition, esketamine use was not associated with a significant increase in hospital or PACU stay, indicating no apparent adverse effect on postoperative recovery.

Several limitations warrant consideration when interpreting these findings. First, substantial clinical heterogeneity was observed regarding dosage regimens, administration timing of esketamine across included studies. Variations in dosing regimens and timing of administration may affect drug efficacy and patient outcomes. Second, our meta-analysis pooled studies using different POD assessment instruments and varying assessment timeframes. This pooling approach implicitly assumes equivalence across these different assessment methods, which may not be fully justified. These instruments have different sensitivities and measure somewhat different constructs, and timing dramatically affects POD detection rates. Third, inclusion of diverse surgical procedures, encompassing cardiac and non-cardiac surgeries, introduced clinical heterogeneity that might influence POD incidence. Finally, the overall risk of bias assessment identified six studies as having unclear or high risk, highlighting potential methodological limitations warranting further improvement.

The most important limitation of this meta-analysis is the geographic concentration of the included studies, which introduces uncertainty regarding the generalizability of the findings to other healthcare settings. This concern extends beyond potential differences in effect sizes across country; rather, it raises the question of whether conclusions derived predominantly from a single healthcare context can be readily applied to Western or other culturally and structurally distinct healthcare systems. Several systemic factors may contribute to this concern and could plausibly influence the observed treatment effects. First, anesthesia protocols differ across healthcare systems, including variation in routine co-interventions such as propofol-based total intravenous anaesthesia, regional techniques, and multimodal analgesia, all of which may independently affect the risk of POD. Second, practices for detecting POD vary considerably. In this review, most Chinese studies assessed POD using the CAM-ICU or CAM-ICU, whereas POD may be underdetected in resource-constrained or non-intensive care perioperative settings elsewhere. Third, patient population characteristics may differ, including baseline frailty, comorbidity burden, and exposure to preoperative benzodiazepines or anticholinergic medications. Fourth, the predominance of single-center trial designs and inconsistent reporting of funding sources among Chinese studies may raise concerns about investigator independence and potential publication pressure, which could inflate effect estimates. Therefore, large-scale, international, multicenter RCTs conducted beyond East Asia are warranted to validate these findings across diverse healthcare systems and patient populations.

Although our findings suggest potential neuroprotective effects of esketamine, its use must be balanced against known risks, including hallucinations, dysphoria, increased sympathetic activity, and the potential exacerbation of delirium in susceptible individuals. These concerns may be particularly relevant in elderly surgical patients and in those with preexisting psychiatric or cerebrovascular conditions. Additional well-designed RCTs are needed to clarify which surgical populations may benefit most from these interventions. Future investigations should also define optimal dosing strategies and timing of administration, including identification of the minimum effective dose that reduces POD while maintaining adequate perioperative analgesia and hemodynamic stability. In addition, well-designed RCTs using validated and standardized neurocognitive assessment instruments with extended follow-up are required to confirm these findings and to inform evidence-based clinical practice regarding the role of esketamine in perioperative neurocognitive protection.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The present meta-analysis provides moderate-certainty evidence suggesting that perioperative esketamine administration may reduce the incidence of POD. The comparable hospital and PACU lengths of stay observed between the intervention and control groups indicate that esketamine does not adversely affect the course of postoperative recovery. Future well-designed, large-scale RCTs using standardized neurocognitive assessment instruments and targeting high-risk surgical populations are warranted to further clarify the neuroprotective efficacy of NMDA receptor antagonists on perioperative neurocognitive outcomes.
